newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Elections give U.S. boost over Bunds.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Elections give U.S. boost over Bunds.

text.p: Profit-taking may temporarily take the post-election glow off U.S. Treasuries but the market is set to outperform German Bunds into next year, analysts said on Wednesday.
With elections on Tuesday maintaining the political status quo and the U.S. economy starting to gear down, Treasuries can continue to narrow the 10-year yield spread against Bunds, analysts said.

"I would expect that spread to go back to flat by the end of the first quarter next year but short term, we've had some soft economic data out from Germany, we've broken out of the top end of the range on the Bund and U.S. bonds have done as much as they possibly can," said Paul Meader at Matheson Investment Management in London.
"In the short-term you may well see 50 or 55 but that I think would be a good buying opportunity," Meader, who manages 200 million stg in fixed income for Matheson.
The spread was quoted at 45 basis points at 1326 GMT.
The results of the U.S. elections were about as positive as debt markets could hope for -- barring a Republican upset, analysts said.

They returned Democrat Bill Clinton to the White House as president but crucially kept the Republicans in control of Congress from where they could continue to keep vigil on any perceived Democratic fiscal excess.
"Everything is in place for Treasuries to outperform," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust in London.

"They seem to be in the process of moving to a lower trading range in terms of the yield," Amstad said. He said a range of 6.25 percent to 6.75 percent on the long bond was sensible. It was quoted at 6.580 percent by early afternoon in Europe.
Meanwhile it was difficult for 10-year German Bund yields to get much below 6.0 percent as domestic support traditionally begins to dry up below that psychological barrier.
"Any such floor doesn't exist (for yields) in the Treasury market," Amstad said. "That's an argument for the spread to narrow."

Ifty Islam, European bond strategist at Merrill Lynch in London, said longer term, the T-note/Bund spread was likely to converge as growth and inflation began to nudge up in Germany next year but pull back in the U.S.
Bunds would also suffer as enthusiasm over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) pulled money away from German markets towards high-yielding targets instead.
"You will tend to see German assets, both the mark and German bonds, devalued over time," he said. "That will also lead to spread narrowing."
This type of trade will be supported by the weakening mark, which will in turn prod German growth, he said.

"This is a virtuous circle for EMU optimists," he said. "The fact that EMU is more likely to happen will weaken the Deutschemark which will in turn improve the German growth outlook and, which in turn makes the whole Maastricht process a little more robust," he said.
Islam said the next target for the T-note/Bund spread would be 30 basis points, the narrowest point since August 12.

But Meader said it would not be all plain sailing for Treasuries with the Federal Open Market Committee set to meet November 13. "I still don't think we're out of the woods yet on U.S. rates," he said.

"We're still growing slightly above trend so the Fed is going to be sensitive to any further signs of growth," he said. He added there was still a chance rates could rise but it was unlikely to come at this meeting.
